match.reason: No single bank point covers the full list of farming impacts (land clearing, erosion, salinity, fertiliser pollution, river overuse and biodiversity loss) at Stage 5 depth for NSW. The closest points each cover only part of it, are aimed at other year levels, or are framed around production in general or the Murray-Darling Basin, so adapting one would need new content rather than small changes.

draft.title: Environmental impacts of food production
card: Growing food changes the land and water around a farm. These changes are called environmental impacts, and farming can cause several of them.
Land clearing and erosion
Clearing native vegetation removes habitat. Without roots to hold soil, wind and rain can wash or blow topsoil away. This is soil erosion.
Salinity
In some regions, clearing deep-rooted plants lets the water table rise. It can bring salts to the surface, and the salty soil makes it hard for crops to grow. This is salinity.
Water impacts

Fertiliser can wash into rivers and cause water pollution. Taking too much water from a river for irrigation is overuse, and it can leave less for river life. Loss of habitat and polluted water can reduce biodiversity, the variety of living things.
draft.remember: Farming can harm land, water and wildlife, through clearing, erosion, salinity, pollution and overuse of rivers.

a.q: After a farmer clears a hillside of trees and grass, heavy rain washes much of the topsoil into a creek. What is this impact called?
a.why: Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil by wind or water, which is more likely when roots no longer hold the soil. Salinity is the tempting wrong answer: it involves salt reaching the surface, not soil being washed away.
a.clue: Think about what the roots were holding in place.

b.q: Farms upstream of a town use fertiliser on their crops. After a storm, the river below turns green with algae and fish numbers fall. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Too much water taken from the river
Rising salts in the soil near the river
Trees cleared from the nearby hills
b.why: Fertiliser washing into a river is water pollution from farming. Overuse of a river is the tempting wrong answer, but it means taking too much water, not adding substances to it.
b.clue: Look at what the farms put on their crops, and where it can end up.

problems.detail: The stem says the farms use fertiliser, and the right option is the only one that repeats that word. The clue then points straight to it, so a student can pick it by word-matching without knowing what water pollution from fertiliser is.

proposal.title: Environmental impacts of food production
card: Land clearing and erosion
Clearing native vegetation removes habitat. Without roots to hold it, topsoil can be washed or blown away by rain and wind. This is soil erosion.
Salinity
In some regions, clearing deep-rooted plants lets the water table rise. It can bring salts to the surface, and the salty soil makes it hard for crops to grow. This is salinity.
Water pollution
Rain can wash fertiliser off paddocks into rivers. The fertiliser feeds algae, which can turn the water green and harm fish.
Overuse and biodiversity
Taking too much water from a river for irrigation is overuse, and it can leave less for river life. Clearing, pollution and overuse can all reduce biodiversity, the variety of living things.
proposal.remember: Farming can harm soil, water and wildlife through clearing, erosion, salinity, pollution and river overuse.

a.q: After a farmer clears a hillside of trees and grass, heavy rain washes much of the topsoil into a creek. What is this impact called?

a.clue: Think about what the roots were holding in place.

b.q: Wheat farms line a river. After heavy rain, water runs off the paddocks into the river. Days later the river turns green with algae and fish die. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Fertiliser carried off the paddocks into the river
Too much water pumped out of the river for crops
Salt rising to the surface of the paddocks
Topsoil blown off the paddocks by strong wind
b.why: The rain carried fertiliser off the paddocks, and it fed the algae that turned the river green. This is water pollution from farming. Overuse is the tempting wrong answer, but it means taking too much water out of a river, not adding something to it.
b.clue: Think about what the rain carried off the paddocks, and what algae need to grow.

b.best: Fertiliser carried off the paddocks into the river
